summary: Defines Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution, which lets hosts resolve names on a local link when conventional DNS is unavailable. It supports DNS formats but uses a separate port and its own resolver cache. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If there is no phone book, you shout the name across the room and the right computer answers. LLMNR does that on a local network so machines find each other by name.

how does link-local multicast name resolution work

subtitle: Name resolution on local networks when DNS is unavailable.

tldr.problem: Devices on a local network need to resolve names when DNS servers are unavailable or unconfigured, but the network has no centralized naming service.
tldr.mechanism: Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) lets hosts shout their name queries to the local link via multicast, and hosts authoritative for those names respond via unicast, using the DNS packet format on a separate port.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can resolve names within their local network segment without centralized DNS infrastructure, enabling small networks and scenarios like mobile ad-hoc networks to function.

today: RFC 4795 is an Informational RFC describing LLMNR, which is deployed in various operating systems including Windows Vista and later, and in some Linux and network devices. It remains the standard reference for link-local multicast name resolution and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Local Name Resolution Without DNS
sections.content:
Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR), described in RFC 4795, enables hosts to resolve names on a local link (such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi) using multicast when conventional DNS is unavailable. LLMNR uses the same packet format as DNS and supports all DNS record types (A, AAAA, MX, SRV, PTR, and others), but operates on a separate port (5355) with its own resolver cache separate from DNS.

LLMNR is not a replacement for DNS; it is intentionally limited to link-local scope. Queries are sent to link-scope multicast addresses (224.0.0.252 for IPv4 and FF02::1:3 for IPv6) that routers will not forward, preventing LLMNR traffic from flooding the network. This makes LLMNR useful for small networks where devices are not configured with DNS servers, such as home networks, small office networks, and especially scenarios like wireless mesh networks or mobile ad-hoc networks.
sections.plainLanguage: LLMNR lets computers on the same wire or Wi-Fi network ask each other for names without needing a special phone book server. The question goes to everyone on the network, and the right computer answers with its address.

sections.title: How Name Resolution Happens
sections.content:
An LLMNR sender sends a query to a link-scope multicast address (224.0.0.252 for IPv4 or FF02::1:3 for IPv6) on UDP port 5355. The query can request any DNS record type. All hosts on that link receive the multicast query. A responder that is authoritative for the queried name responds by sending a unicast UDP response back to the sender. If no responders are on the link for that name, the sender receives no response, which is treated as if the name does not exist.

Responders are configured with the names and records they serve, typically by synthesizing A and AAAA records for their own IP addresses when they start up or are configured on an interface. When a responder receives a query for a name it is authoritative for, it responds with the requested resource records. For unsupported record types, it responds with an empty answer section. Responders listen on UDP port 5355 for multicast queries and on TCP port 5355 for unicast queries. All responses are sent back to the port from which the query originated.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer shouts a question to everyone: "Who has the address for hostname?" Machines on the network that know the answer shout back directly to you with their addresses. If nobody knows, nobody answers.

sections.title: Handling Name Conflicts and Uniqueness
sections.content:
Since LLMNR is a peer-to-peer protocol on a shared local link, multiple hosts could accidentally be configured with the same name. To prevent this, a responder configured with a UNIQUE name (one that should have only a single owner) verifies uniqueness before responding authoritatively. When a host starts up or is configured with LLMNR on a new interface, it sends an LLMNR query for its own name (with a Conflict (C) bit clear). If it receives a response with the Tentative (T) bit clear (indicating a confirmed name), or if the response comes from a host with a lexicographically smaller IP address, the host MUST stop using that name.

When a sender receives multiple LLMNR responses to a single query, it detects a conflict situation. If one response has the Conflict (C) bit clear, the sender should send another query with the C bit set to alert responders of the conflict. Responders receiving a query with the C bit set do not respond directly, but may start their own conflict verification by querying for the conflicting name. This mechanism allows hosts to detect and gracefully handle naming conflicts that arise when separate network segments merge.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a computer claims a name on the network, it shouts "Is anyone named hostname?" If nobody answers (or the answer comes from a computer with a lower address), it can safely use the name. If two computers end up with the same name, they figure out who should keep it based on their addresses.

sections.title: Security Limitations and Protections
sections.content:
LLMNR operates on the local link, limiting exposure to off-link attackers, but on-link attackers (such as others on the same Wi-Fi network) can exploit the protocol. An attacker can spoof LLMNR responses or inject false records since LLMNR does not require authentication by default. Attackers can poison the LLMNR cache by responding with false information. To mitigate this, LLMNR implementations MUST keep LLMNR responses in a separate cache from DNS, preventing LLMNR spoofing attacks from affecting DNS resolution.

Security measures can be implemented if pre-arranged configuration is possible. LLMNR supports TSIG (Transaction Signature) and SIG(0) for authentication, though these only provide group-level authentication. IPsec with NULL encryption can authenticate queries and responses using pre-shared group keys. DNSSEC validation is possible for LLMNR implementations configured with trust anchors, providing the strongest protection by allowing responders to prove ownership of names rather than just group membership. By default, usage should be limited to single-label names (like "hostname" rather than "hostname.example.com") to reduce spoofing risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on your Wi-Fi could lie and say they are hostname and steal traffic meant for someone else. To stay safe, keep LLMNR answers separate from DNS, use only short names without dots, or add passwords (signatures) that only real computers know.

sections.title: Using LLMNR as a Secondary Name System
sections.content:
RFC 4795 recommends using LLMNR as a secondary (fallback) name resolution mechanism, not the primary one. LLMNR should only be used when DNS is unavailable, not configured, or fails to answer a query. A resolver should try DNS first on all interfaces, exhaust DNS server retries and the searchlist, and only then send LLMNR queries. This prevents LLMNR from being a vector for cache poisoning attacks that could override legitimate DNS answers.

LLMNR can be configured manually or automatically using DHCP options (the LLMNR Enable Option). By default, LLMNR responders should be enabled on all interfaces to allow small networks to function. For dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) hosts, LLMNR is particularly valuable in scenarios where IPv6 is not configured with a DNS server but needs name resolution; IPv6-only hosts may use LLMNR to resolve names when no DHCPv6 server or DNS server is available. Administrators should be aware that LLMNR only operates on a single link; it cannot resolve names across routers or VPN boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Use LLMNR only when DNS is broken or not set up. Try the phone book first; only if it does not work, ask the local network. This keeps LLMNR from being tricked into lying about important names.
